title: Three in four people sided with an obviously wrong group at least once
body: In 1951, Solomon Asch showed groups of eight male students a card with a line and asked which of three comparison lines matched it, an obvious call. But seven of the eight were actors, and on 12 of the 18 trials they all gave the same wrong answer. About a third of the real participants’ answers on those trials went along with the group: **74% conformed at least once**, while 26% never did. Afterwards, a few said they had seen it the group’s way; most knew the answer but did not want to seem out of step.

slides.label: of participants sided with the wrong majority at least once
slides.text: 26% never did. With no group pressure, the error rate was under 1%.

slides.heading: Three ways people gave in
items: Distortion of perception: a few believed the group was right
Distortion of judgement: they decided they must be misreading the lines
Distortion of action: they knew the answer but did not want to stand out

slides.heading: One ally is enough
slides.text: When a single partner in the group gave the correct answers, only 5% of participants went on siding with the majority. Group size mattered less than you might think: pressure rose with one, two or three opponents, but adding a fourth, fifth or sixth made no further difference.

slides.question: What happened when one other group member gave the correct answers?
slides.explanation: A single dissenting partner cut conformity to about 5%. Even a dissenter who gave a different wrong answer cut it to about 9%.
